fields.title: RAG Portfolio Chatbot
fields.one_sentence_summary: A production-ready Retrieval-Augmented Generation chatbot embedded in this Django portfolio that answers questions about Marco's background, projects, and skills in real time.
fields.business_problem:
Recruiters and hiring managers spend limited time on portfolio sites before moving on. A static site forces them to hunt for the information they need. The business problem: how do you give every visitor an on-demand, intelligent guide to your portfolio without manual effort?

This chatbot solves that by combining a curated knowledge base with a RAG pipeline — so visitors can ask natural-language questions and get precise, grounded answers rather than scrolling through pages.
key_features: RAG pipeline: documents are chunked, embedded with OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, and stored in a FAISS vector index
LangChain RetrievalQA chain with a custom system prompt tuned to Marco's portfolio context
Dual interface: full-page chat at /chat/ and a floating widget available on every page
Session persistence via UUID stored in localStorage — conversation context carries across page navigation
Rate limiting: max 20 messages per session enforced server-side (HTTP 429 response)
Full audit trail: every user message and assistant reply saved to ChatMessage model in Django
FAISS index rebuilt on every Render deploy via custom management command (build_rag_index)
Zero CDN dependency for the AI stack — all inference via OpenAI API
fields.role_and_contribution:
Solo project — designed and built end-to-end. Responsibilities included:

- Architecting the knowledge base (5 Markdown files covering background, projects, skills, career, and site navigation)
- Building the LangChain RAG chain with a custom PromptTemplate
- Implementing the Django JSON API endpoint with session tracking and rate limiting
- Writing the AJAX-powered chat widget (widget + full-page view)
- Configuring Render deployment with the FAISS rebuild step in build.sh
fields.biggest_challenge:
Making the RAG system give grounded, accurate answers about a real person without hallucinating. Early iterations of the system prompt would sometimes fabricate details not present in the knowledge base.

The solution was two-fold: (1) a tightly scoped system prompt with an explicit 'if you don't know, say so' instruction, and (2) careful chunking of the knowledge base with 50-token overlap so context windows don't split mid-sentence during retrieval.
fields.what_i_learned:
RAG is deceptively simple to demo and genuinely hard to get right. The quality of the knowledge base content matters far more than the model choice — a well-written, structured Markdown file retrieves better than an unstructured data dump.

I also deepened my understanding of LangChain's retrieval abstractions and the tradeoffs between different vector store backends. FAISS is fast and free but requires manual persistence; a managed vector DB would be the right call for a multi-user production system.

fields.title: n8n Automated Agent Workflow
fields.one_sentence_summary: A no-code/low-code automation workflow built in n8n that chains AI tools, APIs, and data sources to execute a multi-step business process end-to-end without manual intervention.
fields.business_problem:
Many business workflows involve repetitive, multi-step processes — pulling data from one source, transforming it, routing it through an AI model, and pushing results somewhere else. Manually executing these chains is slow, error-prone, and doesn't scale.

This project demonstrates how n8n's visual workflow builder can automate a real business process, with AI nodes (Google Gemini / OpenAI) embedded at the decision points where intelligence is actually needed.
key_features: Multi-step workflow triggered by a webhook or schedule
AI node integrated at a key decision point (classification, summarization, or extraction)
Data transformation between steps using n8n's built-in expression engine
Error handling and retry logic configured at each node
Output routed to a destination (email, spreadsheet, database, or Slack) automatically

fields.title: LangChain Conversational Agent
fields.one_sentence_summary: A tool-augmented LangChain agent that can reason over multiple data sources and take actions — going beyond simple chat to complete multi-step tasks autonomously.
fields.business_problem:
Standard chatbots answer questions but cannot take actions or access live data. This project explores the agent paradigm: an LLM with access to a curated set of tools (web search, document retrieval, calculation) that can plan and execute multi-step tasks to accomplish a goal.

The business motivation: many knowledge-worker tasks involve gathering information from multiple sources, synthesizing it, and producing an output — exactly what a well-designed agent can automate.
key_features: ReAct-style agent loop: Reason → Act → Observe until the task is complete
Custom tool definitions with Pydantic input schemas for type safety
Conversation memory using LangChain's ConversationBufferMemory
Streaming output support for real-time response display
Graceful fallback when a tool call fails or returns no results
[Marco: describe the specific tools you built and the use case]
fields.role_and_contribution:
Solo project — designed the agent architecture, defined the tool schemas, wrote the agent executor logic, and built the demonstration interface.

[Marco: add specifics about your actual agent's purpose and any unique implementation decisions]
fields.biggest_challenge:
Agent reliability — getting the model to reliably select the right tool for a given sub-task and stop looping when it has enough information. Early versions would over-call tools or get stuck in reasoning loops when a tool returned ambiguous output.

The fix: strict tool descriptions, explicit stop conditions in the prompt, and a max_iterations guard on the executor.

[Marco: replace with your real challenge]
fields.what_i_learned:
Agent design is fundamentally about prompt engineering and tool design, not model choice. The single biggest improvement came from rewriting tool descriptions to be explicit about when NOT to use each tool — which immediately reduced spurious tool calls.

fields.title: Campus SkillSwap — Django Web App
fields.one_sentence_summary: A full-stack Django web application that connects university students to exchange skills peer-to-peer — think Craigslist for campus skills, with authentication, search, and messaging.
fields.business_problem:
University campuses are full of students with complementary skills — a data science student who needs help with graphic design, a marketing student who wants to learn Python. There's no structured platform to facilitate these exchanges at scale.

Campus SkillSwap addresses this by providing a marketplace where students can list skills they offer and skills they want, find matches, and coordinate exchanges through an in-app messaging system.
key_features: User authentication: registration, login, profile management with avatar upload
Skill listing CRUD: create, edit, and delete skill offers and requests
Search and filter: find skills by category, availability, and keyword
Match system: express interest in another student's skill listing
In-app messaging: direct messages between matched users
Django admin panel for moderation and user management
Responsive design with Bootstrap 5 for mobile-first access
fields.role_and_contribution:
Solo project — full-stack development from initial ERD through deployment. Responsible for data modeling, view logic, template design, authentication flow, and deployment configuration.

[Marco: add any specific technical decisions or team context if applicable]
fields.biggest_challenge:
Designing the data model for the skill matching system without over-engineering it. The first version had a complex many-to-many relationship that made queries difficult. Refactoring to a simpler Interest model with foreign keys to both listing and user cleaned up the ORM queries significantly.

[Marco: replace with your real challenge from this project]
fields.what_i_learned:
Django's class-based views and the ORM are genuinely powerful when you work with them rather than around them. My biggest productivity gain came from leaning into mixins (LoginRequiredMixin, UserPassesTestMixin) instead of writing manual permission checks in every view.
